pass_a_gloss: And the seven brothers written up in the Maccabean books, whom Antiochus maltreated with scourges and sinews while they remained in the fear of God, will be able to be a finest pattern of robust witness to everyone who would reckon whether he is going to be less than little boys, who not only one at a time endured tortures but also, by having looked on at the outrage done to the brothers, displayed a well-strung firmness of piety. One out of whom, having become, as the writing named him, the spokesman, said to the tyrant: why are you about to question and learn? for we are prepared to die rather than to step over the ancestral laws. And why must one tell what sort of things they endured, frying-pans and caldrons being made fiery, in order that they be tortured in them, each having first suffered different things? For the one of them named spokesman was tongue-cut first; then he was skinned around the head, and thus he carried the scalping as others carry the circumcision because of the divine law, supposing that in this too he fills up a word of God's covenant. And not being satisfied with these, Antiochus cut off his extremities, the remaining brothers and the mother looking on together, punishing with the spectacle the brothers and the mother, and supposing he would move their purpose through things thus reckoned frightening. So then Antiochus, not satisfied with these, ordered him, become useless as to the build of the body through the things by which he first punished, to be brought, breathing, to the fire in the pans and the caldrons, and to be fried. And as the steam was given off, the flesh of the noblest contestant of piety being roasted by the tyrant's rawness, the rest called on each other along with the mother to end nobly, consoling themselves by the reasoning that God oversees these things; for the persuasion that the eye of God is present to those enduring was sufficient to them for endurance; and the contest-master of the athletes of piety called on them, being called on (comforted) himself and, so that I may name it thus, made glad at those rising up against such great toils. It would be timely for us also, having come into such things, to speak their words to ourselves, having this manner thus: the Lord God oversees and in truths is comforted upon us.
pass_b_english: The seven brothers too, recorded in the books of the Maccabees, whom Antiochus tormented “with whips and cords” (2 Maccabees 7:1) as they held fast to the worship of God, can be a most beautiful example of strong martyrdom to everyone who stops to consider whether he means to fall short of mere boys. They endured tortures not only one by one, but by having watched the torment of their brothers they also showed a vigorous steadfastness of godliness. One of them, who had become, as Scripture calls him, their “spokesman”, said to the tyrant: “What are you going to ask and learn? For we are ready to die rather than transgress the laws of our fathers” (2 Maccabees 7:2).

What need is there to tell what they endured when pans and cauldrons were heated red-hot so that they might be tortured in them, each of them having first suffered different torments? The one named their spokesman first had his tongue cut out; then he was scalped, and he bore the scalping as others bear circumcision for the sake of the divine law, thinking that in this too he was fulfilling the word of God's covenant. Not content even with this, Antiochus cut off his extremities “while the rest of the brothers and the mother looked on” (2 Maccabees 7:4), punishing the brothers and the mother with the sight and supposing that by things thought so fearful he would shake their resolve. And so Antiochus, still not satisfied, ordered that the man, made useless in the frame of his body by what he had first inflicted, should be brought still breathing to the fire beneath the pans and cauldrons and fried (2 Maccabees 7:5).

As the vapour rose from the flesh of the most noble athlete of godliness, roasted by the tyrant's cruelty, the rest “urged one another, with their mother, to die nobly”, comforting themselves with the thought that God was watching these things. For the conviction that the eye of God is present to those who endure was enough to give them endurance. And the president of the games for the athletes of godliness encouraged them, being himself comforted and, if I may call it so, gladdened over those who rose up against such great pains. It would be fitting for us too, when we find ourselves in such straits, to say to one another the words they used, which run like this: “The Lord God is watching, and truly he takes comfort in us” (2 Maccabees 7:6).

choices.choice: 2026-11-11: retranslated in full from Koetschau (GCS 2, ch. 23); the old English was a digest: it dropped Origen's challenge not to fall short of boys, the scalping compared with circumcision, the mutilation before the brothers and mother, and his comment that God the president of the games was comforted and gladdened; it also had the first brother 'die praying', which the Greek does not say.

choices.issue: παρεκάλεε (M corrected to παρεκάλει; P and Delarue παρακαλεῖ)

choices.choice: Rendered 'comforted' in both places, so that Origen's comment on God and the brothers' words from 2 Macc 7:6 keep the same verb.
'cut off his extremities' (hands and feet, as in 2 Macc 7:4), not a general 'mutilated'.
